about: The words of the chain sword_smuggle (Data/encounters/chain_sword_smuggle_793.json; Design/content/chains/sword_smuggle.md): Frankish swords going north against the king's bans. Every title, intention, line and label key of its thirteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the two news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Asulf, the lord's man's king (Godfred), the steersman (Aldger), the hand (Ravn) and the mate (Brunger) are the spine's cast; Reginbald the smith, Hrodwin his journeyman, Folcbod the eel fisher, Liafburg his widow and Eilger his son are ordinary invented people. Nothing is quoted: the laws (Herstal 779, the missi's capitulary of 803, Thionville 805, Boulogne 811) and the annal of 810 are given in our own plain words. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The smiths' street

On the smiths' street at Colonia a count's man counts sword blades into a cart, one by one, and makes his mark on a stick for each. When the cart has gone the smith, Reginbald, lifts a hide in the corner of his forge. Under it are four blades the count's man did not count.
For the count's own men, at the count's price. The king's word is that no mail coat leaves the realm. A smith who wants to keep his forge reads swords into it as well.
For the count's own men, at the count's price. No arms go over the border now, mail or blade. The merchant who is found with them loses everything he carries, down to the boat's bailer.
A Frisian. You people look at a blade the way other men look at a cask. You do not ask if it is good. You ask how many the boat will hold.
The count pays at Martinmas, in promises, and less than he said. A Dane pays in weighed silver before the thing is in his hand. These four were never on the stick. Forty-five pennies the blade.
Look under the tang. A hammer in a ring, in twisted wire. That is mine. I put it on all of them. A man should be able to find his work again.

There is a man up the river who has begun to put his whole name in the iron, with a cross before it and a cross behind. Buyers ask for the name now and do not look at the blade. I have a hammer and a ring. It will have to do.
Buy the four blades (180 d) and stow them under the ballast
Buy one, openly, for your own belt (50 d)
Say your boat carries wine and stones, and drink his ale

Reginbald wraps the four in greased hide and ties them with bast. He names a man on the Slie who deals in people and carries a hazel switch. After dark the bundle goes under the ballast stones, and the stones go back as they lay.

A free man may wear a sword, and no toll man can say otherwise. Reginbald fits it with a plain hilt while you wait and tells you a riddle about it that he had from an English buyer. The other three go back under the hide.

His ale is thin and his talk is good. The Danes, he says, pay half again for Rhenish tools, and nobody searches a boat for axes and adzes. You part friends. Somebody at the end of the street watches you go.
Ballast out
The toll man is not alone on the dam at Dorestad. A man of the count's stands beside him with two spearmen, and a boy has been sent for baskets. They mean to have your ballast out, stone by stone.
This is not my doing. I take a tenth of what a man sells. I do not lift his floor.
A Frisian was seen on the smiths' street at Colonia ten days ago, after the count's cart had gone. Your boat came down from Colonia. Stand on the dam, shipman.
The king's word names mail coats. The count has decided it means anything with an edge. I would not argue the difference with a spear at my back.
Since Thionville it is everything aboard, not only the arms. Half to the palace. The other half between the officer and the man who finds. Look how keen he is.
You wear nothing I can take from you. Then you will not mind the stones being moved.
Leave the blades under the stones and let them look
Thirty pennies in the toll man's hand before the spearmen reach the boat
Say the blades were bought for the count's own men, and sell them to him at his price
Lift the boards yourself and show them everything

They take out the top course of stones and the casks, find bilge water and a dead eel, and tire of it. The count's man looks at you a little longer than he needs to. The bundle lies a hand's breadth under where they stopped.

The boy's basket catches on a knot of bast. The count's man unrolls the hide on the dam where every shipman can see, and counts four. The blades are the king's now, the court will hear of the rest, and your boat's name is on a stick in the count's hall.
The toll man remembers that the flood is making and the dam is needed for a wine ship. The count's man is told the boat was searched at Noviomagus. He is not sure he believes it. He goes.

You say it before a stone is lifted: four blades, bought for the count's following, to save his cart a second journey. The count's man pays what the count pays, which is less than you gave. He almost thanks you.
You have the boards up before the baskets come. Stones, casks, bilge. The count's man looks, nods, and loses interest in you. The toll man takes it as a kindness that you made his day short.
What lies under the stones
The men know what lies under the ballast. Nobody told them. The steersman wants it said aloud before the boat is out of Frankish water, and he has waited until the others can hear.
Four blades under the stones. I have counted the ways this ends. In most of them I am standing next to you.
And it is not the blades alone any more. They take the boat's whole lading, and then they ask who steered her.
The Franks made that law because they fear the edge. That is the whole of it, you know. A man who fears a thing pays to be rid of it or pays to have it. Either way somebody is paid.
The king calls the Danes his enemies. He called us that, on the Weser. I would carry.
Promise each man a share of what the blades bring
Have the bundle over the side tonight and say no more of it
Tell the steersman his work is the tide, and yours the cargo

A share is a different thing from a wage, and the men sit differently on the thwarts after it. The steersman says a share of a hanging is still a hanging, and steers. The Northman, who is pleased, gives you a riddle about two dead things that boil a wound-leek.

In the dark of the middle watch the bundle goes over the lee side with a ballast stone tied to it. It makes less noise than a hundred and eighty pennies should. The steersman says nothing, which from him is thanks.
He hears you out, looks at the sky, and puts the helm over a little for the ebb. He does not speak of it again. He does not speak of much else either, that day or the next.
The man with the hazel switch

A stout Dane in a good grey cloak has watched your boat since she touched the strand. He carries a hazel switch and a folding scale. Behind his booth is a pen with people in it. He asks, through nobody, in slow plain words, what else came from the river.
You are from the river. Men from the river bring wine and say they have nothing else. Then they show me what else.
Four. With the hammer in the ring. I know the hand. It is a small lot for so long a road.
Nothing. Then you are honest or you are slow. I have work for either.
Four ounces of silver the blade, on my scale and then on yours. Or three people from the pen for the four: Wends, sound, taken this spring. I do not say a price twice.
The king has burned Reric and brought its merchants here to the Slie. There are more buyers than blades now. That is good for a man with blades.
Sell the four blades for weighed silver
Take three people from his pen for the blades
Sell him no blades, and hear what else he wants

He weighs it twice: cut arm rings, a bent brooch, half a foreign coin with writing like worm tracks. Sixteen ounces. He bends each blade over his knee and watches it come back straight. Then he tells you his name, Asulf, which he had not done before.

A man, a woman and a boy of twelve, tied wrist to wrist with hide rope. Asulf says he keeps kin together when it costs him nothing. They are heathen Wends, which the king's law lets a merchant carry, and they eat like crewmen. What you do with them is your affair.

He is not offended. He wants Rhenish tools, six bundles before the winter, and will pay half again over the price. As you go he says the name Asulf, and that a man who changes his mind knows where the booth is.
A cask with no wine in it
A wine cask stands in Reginbald's forge with its head off. There is straw in it, and tallow, and room for eight blades. His journeyman, Hrodwin, is at the grinding stone and listens with his back.
You came back, and with your boat. So the four went where they were going. Good. Now look at this.
You came back. I heard how it went with the four. Do not tell me. Look at this instead.

Eight, hilted, in straw and tallow, and the head pitched on like any other. It is how the big houses send them. There is one at Dorestad who has done it for ten years and has never had a cask opened. Fifty pennies the blade.
Hear this before you say yes. They keep a boat at the river mouth now, with a captain who likes to hear ballast move. He opens casks. Go out on a dark ebb, or do not go out with this.
Every man with twelve farms must own a mail coat now, by the emperor's word, or lose the farms. So the lords take every ring of mail I can make, at their price. I have not been paid since Easter.
The abbey's steward has old mail and nine swords in a chest and may no longer sell them to any stranger. He cannot say so, and he cannot stop saying so.
When you are there, ask something for me. Ask what a smith is worth among them. Not his work. The man.
Buy the cask of eight (400 d)
Carry his lawful iron instead: six bundles of tools (90 d)
Buy nothing, and promise the boy to ask his question in the north
The head is pitched on and the cask is rolled to the strand between two that do hold wine. It rolls like the others. Only its sound is wrong, if a man thinks to knock on it.

Axes, adzes, shears and spoon bits, six bundles tied with bast. Reginbald sells them the way a man sells his second-best ale. Nobody on the river will look twice at them, and the Dane asked for them by name.
Reginbald puts the head back on the empty cask and says the offer will keep until someone else takes it. Hrodwin walks with you to the strand and says nothing more, having said it once.
The watch boat

A long boat with a painted shield at her stem stands out from the river mouth under twelve oars. A man in her bows calls on you to lie to. To seaward the shoals are breaking white, with a channel through them that a small boat might know.
The count's watch. Drop your sail and lie to.
The king's coast watch. Drop your sail and lie to. We are here for Northmen, and for what goes to them.
I know this boat. They cut her on a stick at Dorestad. Today we look at all of her.
Ballast, bilge, and every cask sounded with a mallet. If it rings like wine, you sail on with my blessing.
Lie to with an empty conscience and let them look
Lie to, with the cask standing among the wine
Put her over the shoals where a long boat cannot follow
Roll the cask over the lee side while their sail hides you, then lie to
They sound the casks, lift two stones, and find a merchant's lading. The captain says it is a dull thing to search an honest boat and wishes you a fair wind. He means both.

The mallet goes down the tier. Your steersman has the fourth cask wedged tight between two full ones, with a wet sail thrown over it, and the mallet finds it dull enough. The long boat backs her oars and lets you go.

The fourth cask does not ring like wine. They stave the head in on your own thwart. Eight hilts in straw. The captain takes the blades, sixty pennies for his trouble, and the look of your boat, which he will know again.
She goes over the tail of the bank with a hand's breadth under her and the long boat's oars stop at the white water. They shout something. It is your boat's description, and they have it right.

She touches. Not hard, but long enough for twelve oars. They take what they find, and eighty pennies for the chase, and the captain tells you the day you are to stand before the count. A boat that runs is a boat they remember.

The cask goes in on the side away from them and sinks like the iron it is. When they come aboard there is a gap in the tier the width of one cask. The captain looks at the gap, and at you, and can make nothing of either.
The net and the fish

Asulf has a guest at his booth: a tall man with gold on his arm who does not say whose man he is and does not need to. He wants blades. When that is settled he wants something more, and Asulf leaves the two of you to it.
This one buys for a lord with many ships. He will take every blade you can bring, this summer and the next. I take a tenth for the introduction. I say so now.
This one still carries nothing. A careful man. Careful men live long enough to hear offers.
My lord has forty men who will follow him and nine swords among them. The rest carry axes and hope. You see the trouble.
The king counts his ships against the emperor's, and he is content. Then he counts swords, and he is not.

Blades are fish. We buy them one at a time and they are eaten. I would sooner have the net. Bring the man who makes them, and he shall have a house by the water, iron, charcoal, and nobody over his hearth but one lord.
You asked what a smith is worth here. You have heard it. It is more than a count gives him, and he would have to live among us to spend it.
Sell the eight blades from the cask
Sell six bundles of Rhenish tools, and no blades
Sell nothing; hear the offer out and drink with them

The tall man draws each blade, looks along it, and bends it until the point nears the hilt. All eight come back straight. He pays five ounces the blade without a word about the price. The swords go up the strand in the arms of eight men who did not have one that morning.

Asulf buys the tools himself, for the shipwrights, and pays well. The tall man watches a bundle of adzes change hands as if it were a slight. Then he makes his offer for the smith anyway. He has decided you know the street.

You drink their ale, which is better than a Frank's, and listen. By the end of the evening you have a good deal of their speech, the price they would give for Rhenish wine, and an offer for a man who is not yours to sell.
The mark below the hilt

Men stand round a small boat on the landing with their hoods off. A dead man lies in her on his own nets: Folcbod, who set eel traps in the outer channels. The sword that killed him was left in him, and his wife has drawn it out and holds it across her two hands.

This year a fleet of two hundred ships came from the land of the Northmen to Frisia. The islands off the coast were wasted, the Frisians were beaten in three fights, and a hundred pounds of silver were paid them as tribute.
Three ships lay in the outer channel for water, the men say, and wanted a sail. They were gone on the next tide. Nobody will write it down.
He would not let go of the sail. They left this in him. It is worth more than the sail and the boat. They must have been in haste.
A hand's breadth below the hilt, in twisted wire, is a hammer in a ring.
You have held this blade, or its brother. It went north under your ballast or in your cask, and you were paid for it in silver weighed twice.
You did not sell this blade. You have stood in the forge it came from, you know who carries for that forge and how, and you have told nobody.
You are a merchant. You know marks. Whose is it?
Is it ours now?
Tell her whose mark it is, and all you know of how it came here
Tell her, and lay a hundred pennies on the thwart toward the man's price
Say only that it is Frankish and good, and buy it from her (60 d)

You tell her: a smith at Colonia, a road down the river, a booth on the Slie, and where you stood on that road. She hears it to the end. Then she says that she asked whose mark it was and has had more answer than she wanted, and turns back to the boat.

You tell her, and count a hundred pennies onto the thwart beside the dead man's hand. It is not his price. The men who owe that are at sea. She does not thank you and she does not push it away. The boy counts it after you, moving his lips.

You say it is Frankish work and good, and that she should not keep it in the house. She sells it to you for sixty pennies and is glad to see it go. It lies in your boat under a sailcloth. The men step round it.
What lies between

The king's men are at Dorestad, asking who carries blades north. They sit in the count's hall with a clerk and a bundle of tally sticks. They know a street in Colonia and a booth on the Slie, and this morning a spearman came down to the dam and asked for you by your boat.
They have come as the king's men come now, two together, a count and an abbot, both strangers to this river, so that nobody here has fed them or is their cousin.
A letter has come from the palace, and the count has a stranger at his elbow who reads it to him and watches how he listens.
We have a forge at one end and a dealer in people at the other. We lack what lies between. You sail between.
We have a forge at one end and a dealer in people at the other. And between them, cut on a stick, we have your boat.
Half to the palace. Of the other half, a part to the officer and a part to the man who finds. The emperor has thought about what makes men find.
The king rewards a service. He also remembers the lack of one. I would not want to be remembered so.
Whatever you say in there, say it once and the same way. They ask everything twice.
Give them the road: the forge, the cask, the booth on the Slie
Tell them nothing, go up the river by night and take the smith north
Tell them what you did and what you saw, and take the blade to Saint Martin's
Say you carry wine, and go on carrying blades

You give it all: the hide in the corner, the cask with straw in it, the wine shipper in the lower town who fills the casks for others, the hazel switch. The clerk cuts it on three sticks. The count says to be at the court in forty nights, and to bring a bag.

You tell them you carry wine and are sent away to think. That night you are on the river, rowing against it. Reginbald hears you out with his hands black to the elbow. He takes his hammers, his tongs, his wire, and a bag of his own charcoal, which makes you laugh, and him not.

You tell them what you carried, if you carried, and what you saw, and that you are done with it. You name no names they do not have. The count looks at the abbot, and the abbot says a man who lays a thing down should lay it somewhere. He names Saint Martin's at Traiectum.
Wine, you say, and stones, and cloth. They ask it twice and get it twice the same. You are let go. On the dam the toll man does not look at you, which is the kindest thing he can do.

Wine, you say. The second time you say wine and stones. The clerk cuts something on a stick. You pay sixty pennies for wasting a court's morning, and your boat goes on the list of those to be looked at twice.
The river's man

Asulf has ale on the board and the lord's man beside him. They have counted, between them, what your boat has brought north, and what she could bring in ten summers. They mean to keep you, and they have thought about how.
There was a road from the river with many feet on it. Now there are fewer. The Franks have been pulling men off it. You are still here. So you are the road.
There is a plot by the water, six paces of strand and back to the wall, with my lord's peace on it. No man may draw iron there. Even ours.
They tell me a blade of yours was left in a Frisian. Blades are left in people. It is what they are for. You bought it back, I hear. That was tidy.
They tell me you told a widow whose blade killed her man. That was honest, and it was not wise. Her kin can count. Do not sleep ashore in Frisia.
The king forbade it again, and his son after him, and his grandson on pain of death. The blades went north all the same.
Take the plot by the water and the lord's peace on it
Take silver and a guest's seat, and no house the Franks can name

Four posts are driven and a rope is run between them, and that is a house plot on the Slie. Asulf weighs out the silver that was owing and lays three marten skins on it for luck. On the Rhine they will hear that a Frisian has a house among the Danes. On the Frisian coast a family knows whose cargo it was.

You take the silver, more of it, and a seat at the lord's board whenever your boat is on his strand. No posts are driven. A man with no house here can still say, at Dorestad, that he sells wine. On the Frisian coast a family knows better.
The finder's share

At the count's court at Dorestad a clerk reads out what was taken: a cask of blades opened on the dam, a forge at Colonia sealed with the count's seal, a wine shipper of the lower town in irons. Then he reads your name, and every shipman on the river turns to see whose it is.
Item, twenty-three swords and four mail coats. Item, one boat. Item, wine to the number of thirty casks. Item, the said shipper's house and dam.
Half to the palace. Of the rest, the officer's part and the finder's part. It is the law, and it is weighed here before the court so that nobody can say it was not paid.
No law yet says what the finder is owed. So it is the king's grace, and I am to be generous with it. I have been told how generous.
The smith is too good to waste. He goes to the palace forges with his tools. He will make blades for the rest of his life and never sell one. Unless somebody here speaks for him.
There is a bigger house on this river that we did not touch. We had no cask of his. Men like that are never found with the cask.
This year the road by which swords went from Colonia to the Danes was closed. The next year there was another.
Take the finder's share, weighed out before the court
Take a third of it, and ask that the smith keep his forge and his hands

Sixteen hundred pennies, weighed, and a strip of parchment with the king's name on it: your goods pass the toll at Dorestad free, and your house is under his protection. Reginbald goes up the river in a cart with his tools. Nobody on the dam drinks with you that night. On the Slie a man with a hazel switch will hear how it was done.

You take a third and say the smith only sold what the count would not pay for. The abbot likes the answer. Reginbald keeps his forge, with a count's man counting every blade out of it, and the parchment with the king's name is yours all the same. On the Slie a man with a hazel switch will hear how it was done.
A forge on the Slie

There is a new house by the water at Sliesthorp, with a turf roof and a smoke that is not a cooking smoke. Reginbald is at the anvil in a borrowed apron. The lord's man sits on a chopping block and watches him work, as he has every day since the boat came in.
He came north in your boat between two casks, with a sail over him at Dorestad and at the river mouth. He was sick the whole way and complained only of the damp in his charcoal.
Their iron is bog iron and comes in lumps like bread. Their charcoal is birch. I said it could not be done. It can be done. It takes twice as long, and I have nothing else to do.
Hrodwin has the forge at Colonia and my mark with it. He will tell the count's men I fell in the river. He has wanted to say that for years.
I said a house, iron, charcoal and one lord. He has asked for a second bellows and a boy who does not talk. He shall have them. Men have been given land for less than what he is making.
This is the first. Look under the tang. The same hammer, the same ring. A man should be able to find his work again, wherever he has had to do it.

No book in Francia tells of this. In the north they said afterwards that the good blades began on the Slie in those years, and that the first smith there was a foreigner who never learned to like the ale.
Take a third of the forge's work to sell, and keep your goods in his house
Take the first blade and the lord's purse, and no part in what follows

You shake hands on a third. His house will hold your goods between voyages, and nobody steals from the lord's smith. The lord's man weighs out eight hundred pennies' worth for the bringing of him. Blades are cheaper on the Slie from this year. On the Rhine your name is on a stick beside his.

He gives you the first blade himself, hilted in the northern way, because the hilt was all they would let anyone else make. The lord's man weighs out the purse. You have sold a man his freedom and a king his swords, and it is hard to say which of them paid more. On the Rhine your name is on a stick.
Iron for the saint

The blade lies on a linen cloth before the altar of Saint Martin at Traiectum, with the hammer in its ring turned upward. The dead man's widow, Liafburg, has come up the river with her son to see what is done with it. The priest has not yet touched it.
Iron given to the saint is the saint's. The smith here will draw it out into a strap for the west door. Men will go in past it for as long as the door stands, and none of them will know.

A man who has laid one trade down wants another. The saint has wine to carry down to Dorestad, and his men pay no toll on the banks there. The steward will pay your freight before you sail. He does that for nobody.
You paid toward him when you owed nothing by law. I have not forgotten it. I have not forgiven the rest of it yet. One thing at a time.
I came to see it done. I did not come to make it easy for you.
My father's boat is too big for me and my mother has sold the traps. Do you need a boy who can scull?
This year a merchant of Dorestad gave a sword to Saint Martin, and it was made into a hinge.
Take the boy aboard as your fosterling, and carry the saint's wine
Leave the boy with his mother, pay his keep to the church, and carry the saint's wine

Liafburg puts the boy's hand in yours before the altar and says his name and his father's name, so that the saint has heard it. Eilger comes aboard with a bundle and an eel spear. The steward counts out the freight. Your house is Saint Martin's man now, and the toll men on the banks know the saint's mark on a cask.

The boy stays with his mother, and a hundred and twenty pennies go into the church's chest for his bread until he is grown. He looks at your boat as you go down to her. The steward counts out the freight. Your house is Saint Martin's man now, and the toll men on the banks know the saint's mark on a cask.

This year, at the count's court at Dorestad, a wine shipper of the lower town was found to have sent swords to the Danes in casks. His goods were taken, half for the palace. A forge at Colonia was sealed. The Danes are paying half again for any blade they can get.
This year a Frankish smith set up his forge at Sliesthorp, under a lord of the Danes, and made swords there with his own mark. A blade is cheaper on the Slie than it has been in any man's memory.

Inside a dark forge on the smiths' street at Colonia, late afternoon: a broad grey-bearded smith in a leather apron lifts a hide from four bare sword blades in a corner; through the open door behind him a count's cart rolls away up a street of low workshops under the old Roman wall.

The dam at Dorestad on a grey morning: a Frank in a red cloak points into a small open boat while a boy carries ballast stones up in a basket and two spearmen wait; the toll man stands aside with his tally stick, looking at the river.

The small boat under sail at dusk on brown water, four men aboard: the steersman at the side rudder speaking without turning his head, an old Northman smiling at the bilge, a big Saxon with folded arms; the ballast stones at their feet.

A beach market in the north, a clear cold noon: a stout Dane with a plaited beard and a hazel switch holds up a small folding scale; behind his booth a wattle pen with people sitting in it, and boats drawn up on the sand.

The forge at Colonia by firelight: a wine cask with its head off, straw spilling from it and eight sword hilts showing; the smith with one hand on the rim, and behind him a young man at a grinding wheel, his back turned, his head tilted to listen.

A river mouth in a fresh breeze under a broken sky: a long twelve-oared boat with a painted shield at her stem bears down on the small merchant boat; white water on the shoals to seaward, low dunes behind.

Evening at a booth on the Slie: a tall Dane with gold arm rings bends a sword blade into a bow across his knee by lamplight, watching the merchant and not the blade; the stout dealer stands back in the doorway; ships' prows dark against the water.

A Frisian landing at low water under a flat white sky: a small boat on the mud with a dead man laid on his nets; a woman in a dark cloak holds a sword level across both hands toward the viewer, a boy of ten at her side; men with their hoods off stand around.

The count's hall at Dorestad, daylight from the door: a Frankish count and an abbot sit side by side on a bench with a clerk and a bundle of tally sticks before them; the merchant stands alone on the rushes; a spearman at the door post.

The strand at Sliesthorp on a bright windy day: four posts and a rope mark a plot of sand by the water; the stout dealer weighs cut silver on his scale and lays three marten skins beside it; longships lie along the shore behind.

The count's court at Dorestad held in the open by the dam: a scale with a heap of silver pennies on a board, a clerk reading from a strip of parchment, a man in irons at one side, and a ring of shipmen all looking at the merchant.

A turf-roofed forge by the water at Sliesthorp in the blue light of a northern evening: the Frankish smith at the anvil holds up a new blade to look along it, sparks at his feet; a tall Dane sits on a chopping block watching; the fjord and the boats beyond.

Inside the small stone church of Saint Martin at Traiectum, morning light from one window: a sword on a white cloth before the altar, a priest with his hands not yet on it, and a woman in a dark cloak with a boy who is looking back at the merchant.
